boards.description:
## Intro

I'm new to this application, but the goal is to have a loose scrum-inspired KanBan board
as plain-text data living inside the code repository.

I imagine a PR that defines & refines the tasks & stories it works on, as well as the code
it changes. This decouples project planning from any single planning/management/code forge
platform, as well as allowing comfy terminal UI & nvim editing. The code forge could even
have automated checks on the work items as well as the code, to ensure quality. (Though
this risks becoming a very perverse incentive.)

I'd like something a little more human-readable than JSON as a backend, but I'll see how
it goes. At least Nushell makes any structured data convenient to work with.

## Glimmer (Better Name Pending)

I mostly want to experiment with Gleam web development. I was a little naive going into
this, as it turns out that a full-stack Lustre application with SSR & client-side
hydration is a little complicated, but I'm excited to try it out.

There's some really cool paradigms here, that I feel could be very powerful. I'm a little
worried about Lustre's "Model - Update - View" single global state and pure function
architecture's performance, but we'll see. Not that I ever have or ever will make anything
important enough that performance becomes a concern...

The rough idea for the project is to make an appointment, dossier, and billing management
website for healthcare professionals. Inspired by some recent trouble my mother
experienced in her line of work.

It sounds a little big, but I basically just want:

- A calendar where you add appointments.
- Some free-text notes attached to patients.
- And a billing editor where you can add and tweak order line items to generate a PDF
  (eventually).

Long-term goals could be things like multi-tenancy and franchising:

- Managing a stock of available products that can be sold by franchisees.
- Gathering insights on the performance of the franchisees.
- Rescheduling patients across franchisees.
- Secure communication.
- E-mailing.
- Integration with bookkeeping software.
- Automatic reminders: Patient needs to answer a questionnaire, visit the lab, products
  restocked etc.

## Conventions

My project planning is heavily influenced by my educational experience. Planning is
basically Kanban, because I'm not committing to sprint deadlines for a casual personal
hobby project (yet). But task ontology is intended to follow Open-ICT's model:

- Epic: Family of related steps in the user journey (vertical slice, see journey mapping)
- Feature: A specific functionality, part of an Epic.
- Story: A concrete unit of (multidisciplinary) work implementing (part of) a Feature.
  - Learning story: work item for acquiring requisite skill for a work item.
  - Research story: work item where the result is new knowledge, typically in the form of
    a decision.
- Task: The lowest common denominator of work items: a story has a list of tasks. Disperses
  task between team members of different disciplines. A task is less than a day's work.

Work items are written in the

> "**As A** <stakeholder> **I want** <functionality> **So that** <motivation>"

formulation. This way story items stay consistent and focused on the
interests of the users and/or stakeholders.

Work items have _Acceptance Criteria_ (When is the work complete?) and _quality criteria_
(When is the work good?)

cards.description:
## Gleam web dev

Lustre full-stack applications are monorepos consisting of a client, server, and shared
library. I want some basic hello-world level placeholder code for each of this to showcase
what the code and file structure looks like and what the fundamental pieces are.

## Database

For data storage I'll need a database of some variety. I'm partial to PostgreSQL, even
though SQLite has extreme reliability.

I might try Gel out again, because the object-graph-relational hybrid model and custom DSL
seem really cool. Didn't super like how they implemented their own local dev hosting stuff
though. Too opinionated in how they automatically install and set up stuff on your
machine. And getting it to work with Gleam might be outside my power. Don't even know if
a connector library exists for Gleam.

Maybe I should research if there's something that works particularly well with the kind of
calendar features I need. I don't think the relational model is that useful for orders.
Prices change over time, that shouldn't affect orders that were long since paid.

## Testing & CI

Apart from that, I need some testing: Unit testing for each individual project, and some
sort of integration test for the whole thing together. I'd like to get into more advanced
forms of testing, but that's for another story.

I really liked using `hurl` in a previous project. Maybe I'll have a use for that again.
But from what I've seen, Wisp includes _really nice_ test helpers for simulating requests,
so that kind of overlaps in functionality. Although I think asserting things parsed from
HTTP responses might have a little nicer syntax in `hurl` than with
`wisp.simulate_browser`. But that is also only the plain JSON/HTML responses from the
server, if I want to assert things about the interactive elements of the UI (if and when
I ever get to that), I might need something more advanced. I hope `hurl` can do that, and
I won't need some puppeteer or headless chrome or whatever nonsense.

I'll want some CI/CD with GitHub actions. To run lints and tests, but I'd also like to
build and publish an artifact of sorts.

## Artifacts & CD

Docker-compose for local development might also be a good thing. I'd love to build the
images using Nix, but I don't think that pairs well with docker-compose. Docker-compose
for local development is a little redundant if you already have a reproducible Nix dev
shell. So maybe I'll think on that a little harder. Docker-compose is a little more
approachable for people that aren't already Nix-pilled though.

I think it might also be possible to bundle/package the application as some sort of
Erlang/beam artefact. Although I bet combining the JS client stuff is complicated. It
would be cool to make it reproducible with Nix, and automate it with CD and publish it
somewhere.

cards.description:
As a user
I want secure HTTP headers
in order to have basic protection against XSS

## As Is

There is basically no foundation yet for the application. Wisp does ship a selection of
middleware to us, one of which is for strict CSP headers.

## To Be

A middleware function that sets a variety of important HTTP response headers that relate
to security, such as `content-security-policy`, with actual values tuned according to
balance security and needs for the application.

Without CSP headers, any injected resource, such as JavaScript will be fetched/executed
without scrutiny. Validation and sanitization is _still required_ to defend against
cross-site scripting.

## Acceptance Criteria

- CSP header present to limit trusted origins for script/style/image sources
- Other headers are also used to increase security profile:
  - <https://github.com/scott-ray-wilson/plume>
  - <https://helmet.js.org/>

## Quality Criteria

- CSP header is tuned for maximum security:
  <https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/CSP>
- Headers are automatically included in HTTP responses from the backend server through
  middleware.

cards.description:
As a developer  
I want the backend server to use the Lustre API to return HTML elements & JSON
In order to have a basic foundation of how to use these parts in the application

## As Is

Empty folder

## To Be

Added `server/` sub Wisp project, using the Lustre library to compose HTML and JSON to
return on different endpoints.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Tech stack is Gleam Lustre+Wisp full-stack
- Folder structure for the server
- Initial code examples showcasing how to parts are going to work together
- GitHub actions workflow present for error / style linting and unit tests

## Quality Criteria

- Follows conventions and best-practices from Gleam and Lustre
- Keeps security in mind
- Keeps extensibility and maintainability in mind
- Uses Git & Jujutsu to keep a linear, patch-oriented, one-thing-at-a-time change history
- Documentation where relevant
